title: Loops and Repetition Checkpoint
intro: Your programs can repeat themselves now: for, while, do-while, break, continue and loops inside loops. Twelve rounds, one from every idea in this module. First-try answers earn three stars!

rounds.prompt: What are the three parts inside a for loop's brackets, in order?
options: The start value, the condition to keep going, and the update after each turn
The start value, the update, and the condition
The condition, the start value, and the number of turns
The start value, the end value, and the step
rounds.explain: The start runs once, the condition is tested before every turn, and the update runs after every turn.

rounds.prompt: How many times does this block run, and what is the last value of i inside it?
rounds.explain: It runs with 0, 1, 2 and 3. The loop stops the moment i reaches 4, so 4 is never used inside the block.

rounds.prompt: This was meant to print three lines and prints one. Why?
options: The semicolon gives the loop an empty body, so the block below is not part of it
A for loop cannot contain a print
rounds.explain: Exactly the same trap as a semicolon after an if. The loop repeats nothing, then the ordinary block below runs once.

rounds.prompt: Why must a running total be declared before the loop rather than inside it?
options: A variable declared inside is created fresh each turn and is gone after the loop
Because Java forbids new variables inside a loop
So the loop can run faster
So it can be used as the counter
rounds.explain: It needs to survive from one turn to the next, and to still exist when the loop has finished.

rounds.prompt: What does this while loop do?
options: Prints i is 1 up to i is 5
rounds.explain: Nothing in the block changes i, so the condition stays true. A while loop's update is your job, and this one is missing.

rounds.prompt: You want to ask for input and keep asking until it is valid. Which loop fits best?
options: do-while, because you have to ask once before you can judge the answer
for, because you know the number of tries
while, because it might need zero turns
Any of them: there is no difference
rounds.explain: The first question is unavoidable, so a loop that always runs once lets you write the prompt and the rule a single time.

rounds.prompt: The condition is false from the very start. What does this print?
rounds.explain: A do-while tests its condition after the block, so the block always gets one turn whatever the condition says.

rounds.prompt: What does this print on one line?
rounds.explain: `continue` abandons only the current turn, so the even numbers are skipped and the odd ones still print.

rounds.prompt: How many numbers does this print before "Done"?
rounds.explain: 1, 2 and 3 print, then `break` ends the loop before 4 is printed. `break` ends the loop, not the program, so Done still appears.

rounds.prompt: How many times does the innermost line run?
rounds.explain: Nesting multiplies: the inner loop runs all four of its turns on each of the outer loop's three turns.

rounds.prompt: Match each tool to the job it fits best.

pairs.right: Repeat a known number of times
Repeat until an event happens, possibly never
Repeat, but run at least once
Skip the rest of this turn only

rounds.explain: Six tools for repetition. Picking the one that matches your intent is what makes a loop readable at a glance.

rounds.prompt: Build a nested loop that prints a growing triangle of stars: one star on the first row, two on the second, and so on.
rounds.explain: The inner limit is the outer counter, which is what makes the rows grow. The println sits inside the outer loop but after the inner one, so exactly one line ends per row.
